title: If not now, when? (Avot 1:14)
hook: Hillel: if I am not for myself, who is; if only for myself, what am I; if not now, when

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hillel told us to be disciples of Aaron, walking between two people until they meet. Your line was pursue peace. Did you carry a kind word across? Day two hundred forty-four.

There's a thing on your list that's been there for weeks. The call to your grandmother. The doctor's appointment. The apology. The form. Every morning it slides down to tomorrow, and tomorrow is always a better day for it. Two thousand years ago, Hillel wrote the shortest possible answer to that list. It's three questions, one line each, and it may be the most quoted sentence in all of Pirkei Avot. People have put it on posters, in speeches, and on the title page of novels. The last question is only four words in English. You probably already know it.
screen: `THE THING ON YOUR LIST.` → `TOMORROW IS ALWAYS BETTER.` → `THREE QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Here is Hillel's saying, in chapter one. If I am not for myself, who will be for me? And when I am for myself, what am I? And if not now, when? Take them one at a time. The first question is about responsibility. Nobody else can live your life, learn your lessons, or do your good deeds for you. Commentators read it this way: if I don't work on myself, no one can do it in my place. It's not selfish. It's a person standing up. The second question turns right around. And when I am only for myself, what am I? A person who lives only for himself shrinks. Hillel doesn't answer the question. He lets it sit there, a little uncomfortable, and lets you fill it in. So the first two lines hold each other in balance. Stand up for yourself. Don't stop there. And then the third line, which gives both of them a deadline. If not now, when? The Hebrew is im lo akhshav, eimatai. Akhshav is the ordinary word for now, the one people use to call a kid to dinner. There's no poetry in it. It means this minute. Some commentators add a sharper reading: now means this life, this world, while you still have time to act. The saying works like a staircase. Care for yourself. Care beyond yourself. Start today. Hillel, who climbed onto a roof in the snow rather than miss one lesson, knew what it meant to not wait for a better day.
screen: `IF I AM NOT FOR MYSELF, WHO?` · `IF ONLY FOR MYSELF, WHAT AM I?` · `IF NOT NOW, WHEN?` · `AKHSHAV: THIS MINUTE.` · then, large: `IF NOT NOW, WHEN?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the delayed thing. Settle, and breathe. Let the list in your head come up, and notice which item has been waiting longest. Don't judge yourself for it. Just look at it. Now make it smaller: what's the very first step, the one that takes two minutes? Opening the email. Finding the number. Writing the first line. Picture yourself doing just that step, right after the bell. The bell holds the time.
If not now. The last of Hillel's three questions: care for yourself, care beyond yourself, and don't wait for a better day.
Your line: if not now, when. Today, take the first two-minute step on one thing you've been putting off. Day two hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Hillel's three questions are among the best-known lines of Pirkei Avot, studied on summer Shabbat afternoons and often quoted in Jewish teaching as a call to act without delay.

notes: Avot 1:14 is given as a paraphrase in our own words (outline follows Taylor 1897), without quotation marks.

The reading of the first question as 'no one can do my good deeds for me' follows classic commentators (e.g. Rashi and Bartenura on Avot); the reading of 'now' as this world is also attributed to commentators; confirm.
'On the title page of novels': Primo Levi's novel 'If Not Now, When?' takes its title from this saying; confirm before adding it by name.
